{{Short description|Sequence of rational numbers}}
[[Image:SuiteSpecker.svg|thumb|200px|A Specker sequence. The ''n''<sup>th</sup> digit of x<sub>''k''</sub> is '''4''' if ''n'' ≤ ''k'' and the ''n''th [[Turing machine]] in a computable [[Gödel numbering]] halts on input ''n'' after ''k'' steps; otherwise it is '''3'''.]]
In [[computability theory]], a '''Specker sequence''' is a [[computable function|computable]], [[Sequence#Increasing_and_decreasing|monotonically increasing]], [[Sequence#Bounded|bounded]] [[sequence]] of [[rational number]]s whose [[supremum]] is not a [[computable real number]]. The first example of such a sequence was constructed by [[Ernst Specker]].{{sfnp|Specker|1949}}  

The existence of Specker sequences has consequences for [[computable analysis]]. The fact that such sequences exist means that the collection of all computable real numbers does not satisfy the [[least upper bound principle]] of real analysis, even when considering only computable sequences.  
A common way to resolve this difficulty is to consider only sequences that are accompanied by a [[modulus of convergence]]; no Specker sequence has a computable modulus of convergence. 
More generally, a Specker sequence is called a ''recursive counterexample'' to the least upper bound principle, i.e. a construction that shows that this theorem is false when restricted to computable reals.

The least upper bound principle has also been analyzed in the program of [[reverse mathematics]], where the exact strength of this principle has been determined. In the terminology of that program, the least upper bound principle is equivalent to ACA<sub>0</sub> over RCA<sub>0</sub>.  In fact, the proof of the forward implication, i.e. that the least upper bound principle implies ACA<sub>0</sub>, is readily obtained from the textbook proof (see Simpson, 1999) of the non-computability of the supremum in the least upper bound principle.

== Construction 1 ==

One way to construct a Specker sequence is as follows:{{sfnp|Kushner|1984}} let ''A'' be any [[recursively enumerable]] set of [[natural number]]s that is not [[decidable set|decidable]], and let (''a''<sub>''i''</sub>) be a computable enumeration of ''A'' without repetition. Define a sequence (''q''<sub>''n''</sub>) of rational numbers with the rule
:<math>q_n = \sum_{i = 0}^n 2^{-a_i - 1}.</math>
It is clear that each ''q''<sub>''n''</sub> is nonnegative and rational, and that the sequence ''q''<sub>''n''</sub> is strictly increasing. Moreover, because ''a''<sub>''i''</sub> has no repetition, it is possible to estimate each ''q''<sub>''n''</sub> against the series
:<math>\sum_{i = 0}^\infty 2^{-i-1} = 1.</math>
Thus the sequence (''q''<sub>''n''</sub>) is bounded above by 1.  Classically, this means that ''q''<sub>''n''</sub> has a supremum ''x''. 

It can be shown that <math>x</math> is not a [[Computable number|computable real number]]. Suppose, to the contrary, that <math>x</math> were computable. Then the sequence <math>(q_i)</math> would have a computable [[modulus of convergence]]: there would be a computable function <math>r(n)</math> such that

: <math>|q_j-q_i|<\frac{1}{n}</math>

for all <math>i,j>r(n)</math>. Such a function can be obtained by approximating <math>x</math> and comparing it with successive terms of <math>(q_i)</math>. Since each new term in the enumeration changes a single digit in the binary expansion, a sufficiently accurate approximation to <math>x</math> determines a stage after which the relevant initial segment can no longer change.

If such a function <math>r</math> were computable, it would provide a [[Decision problem|decision procedure]] for <math>A</math>. Given <math>k</math>, compute <math>r(2^{k+1})</math>. If <math>k</math> were later enumerated into <math>A</math>, the corresponding term would increase the sequence by <math>2^{-k-1}</math>. This cannot occur after all terms with indices greater than <math>r(2^{k+1})</math> are within <math>2^{-k-1}</math> of one another. Therefore, if <math>k</math> belongs to <math>A</math>, it must appear among the first <math>r(2^{k+1})</math> terms of the enumeration. These finitely many terms can be checked effectively, yielding a decision procedure for <math>A</math>. This contradicts the assumption that <math>A</math> is not [[Decidable set|decidable]], so <math>x</math> is not computable.

==Construction 2==
Another construction of a Specker sequence (''x<sub>m</sub>'') can be given using an [[enumeration]] of [[Turing machine|Turing machines]]. Let {''n''}(''n'') denote the action of the ''n''-th Turing machine on the number ''n''. Then let the ''n''-th [[decimal digit]] of ''x<sub>m</sub>'' be 4 if ''m'' > ''n'' and the computation {''n''}(''n'') halts within ''m'' − ''n'' steps. If the computation has not finished after ''m'' − ''n'' steps (or if ''m'' < ''n''), the digit is 3. (See the figure above.)

* Each ''x<sub>m</sub>'' is a [[rational number]], since it has a [[decimal expansion|periodic decimal expansion]]: after the first ''m'' decimal places, all digits are 3.
* The sequence is computable, since to produce ''x<sub>m+1</sub>'' after having calculated ''x<sub>m</sub>'', one only has to simulate ''m'' + 1 Turing machines running for one step each.
* The sequence is increasing, because when passing from ''x<sub>m</sub>'' to ''x<sub>m+1</sub>'', digits can only change from 3 to 4.
* The sequence is bounded, because it never exceeds 0.4444444... = 4/9.

The limit of this sequence is not a [[computable real number]], since its decimal expansion contains a 4 in its ''n''-th decimal place if the computation {''n''}(''n'') halts, and a 3 otherwise. Determining the digits of the limit would therefore solve the [[Halting problem]], which is impossible.
